newsitem.title: USA: White House, Republicans talk compromise on taxes.
newsitem.headline: White House, Republicans talk compromise on taxes.

text.p: Republicans and White House officials began outlining areas of possible compromise on Thursday in trying to bridge differences on a tax cut package.

Capitol Hill was rife with meetings between Republicans, Democrats and administration officials, with negotiators shuttling between Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott's office, House Speaker Newt Gingrich's office and other locales.

House and Senate leaders are trying to strike a compromise with the White House on tax and spending bills that would enact a May agreement to balance the budget over five years and provide $85 billion net tax cuts.

"I think we're making some progress, we're getting serious ... and trying to see if we can't get this deal tied up in a couple of days," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles said. "We started letting them know where we're willing to compromise and vice versa," the Oklahoma Republican added.
The administration also said progress was being made. "We had a very useful discussion around the areas we need to deal with," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said.

House and Senate Republicans earlier this week arrived at a unified tax plan that received a cool reception from the White House. On Thursday, administration officials clearly presented their views on the tax issues.
Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said he put a new proposal on the table related to the tobacco tax but would not give details.

The Senate tax bill includes a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax to raise about $15 billion over five years, $8 billion of which would go to fund children's health programmes. President Clinton has endorsed that approach.

Some Republicans who were not part of the main tax talks said they had heard of a Republican proposal to include the cigarette tax, but not earmark the funds for children's health and were angered by that.
"How in the world can they keep the 20 cents in there and not take care of the kids. To me, that's unbelievable," said Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican.
House Republicans have said there was not much support on their side for a cigarette tax increase, and a Republican aide said no decisions had been made on the tobacco tax.
Gingrich sounded hopeful that compromise would be reached in the major tax areas.

"We had a very good meeting," the Georgia Republican said. "We really do hope to have the educational tax credit ... the $500 per child credit. We also think we will be able to work out the estate tax rates for small businesses and family farms and a cut in the capital gains."

Republicans have rejigged the structure of a $500 per-child tax credit so that it could be kept in a special account for up to three years for low-income families who do not owe income tax after receiving other tax breaks.

Those families would be allowed to receive the child credit once they owed some income tax. The structure of the child credit is a key sticking point with the White House which wants the credit to go to more low-income families, including as a government payment if they owe no income taxes.

The tax and spending talks were expected to continue into the evening. Republicans want to finish the legislation by Aug. 1, while the White House says crafting acceptable legislation is more important than meeting a deadline.
Daschle of South Dakota said Clinton would also keep a close eye on the $115 billion in Medicare spending cuts.

White House Budget Director Franklin Raines discounted chances for increasing the Medicare eligibility age or instituting a $5 copayment for home health services. The administration opposes both those proposals.
Raines said the administration was still working on making Medicare recipients who are better off pay more for doctors.
Aside from those three major Medicare issues, the two sides said they were narrowing differences with a handful of outstanding issues remaining.
Republicans made a compromise offer on welfare that moved toward the White House on providing disability benefits to legal immigrants currently in United States but not on the benefit rolls.
